title: The Gift of Laughing Again
summary: When laughter returns after a heavy season, it does not erase what you carried. It reminds you that sorrow did not get to keep all of you.
excerpt: When laughter returns after a heavy season, it does not erase what you carried. It reminds you that sorrow did not get to keep all of you.
paragraphs: There is a particular kind of laughter that surprises you after a hard season.

It is not polite laughter. Not the small smile you offer because someone expects you to be okay. It comes from somewhere deeper. Someone says something ridiculous, a child does something unexpected, an old friend remembers a story, and before you can stop it, you are laughing properly. Your shoulders move. Your face hurts a little. For a moment, you forget to be careful.
Then you notice it happened.

Part of you may feel almost confused. You may wonder whether you were allowed to laugh that freely after everything that happened. Whether joy means you have moved on too quickly. Whether enjoying a moment makes light of the grief, pressure, disappointment, or exhaustion you have been carrying.
It does not.
Laughter is not disloyal to your pain.

A heavy season can make us forget that we are still capable of delight. We become so used to survival that our body holds everything tightly. We plan for the worst. We speak carefully. We move through the day with only enough energy for what must be done. Even when the difficult thing begins to lift, some part of us stays braced, as if relaxing would make us careless.
Then laughter returns, and it tells the truth before we have words for it.

It says there is still life in you. It says the hard thing did not take every colour from the room. It says the part of you that loved, played, hoped, and responded to joy was not gone. It was simply quiet for a while.
This does not mean the season was not real.

You may still have things to process. You may still be tired. You may still be grieving what changed or did not change. Healing is rarely a clean line from sadness to happiness. It is often a more human mixture: a difficult conversation in the morning, a good laugh at lunch, a tear in the evening, and enough grace to wake up and try again tomorrow.
That mixture is not failure.
It is what it looks like to be alive.

Some of the most hopeful moments are not the ones where all pain disappears. They are the ones where pain no longer gets the final word in every room. Where you can carry the memory and still enjoy the meal. Where you can miss what was lost and still laugh with the people who remain. Where your heart can hold sorrow and gratitude without forcing either one to leave.
If laughter has come back to you lately, receive it as a gift.

Do not analyse it away. Do not apologise for it. Let it remind you that your story is bigger than the chapter that nearly convinced you life would always feel heavy. Let it be a small sign that your heart is still responding to goodness.

And if laughter has not returned yet, do not force it. Joy cannot be commanded like a task. It arrives in its own time, often when we feel safe enough to stop watching the door. Until then, be gentle with yourself. Stay close to people who do not require you to perform recovery. Let ordinary kindness make room for you.
One day, something may catch you off guard.
You will laugh, and for a few seconds you will remember yourself.
Not the version of you from before the hard season, because you have changed. The version of you who made it through and still has the ability to be moved by something good.
Sorrow may have visited you.
It did not get to keep all of you.
